## Abstract

This CHIP defines a standard to enable a scalable voting mechanism on the Chia Blockchain that could achieve the goal of 20,000+ voters.  

This is based on the DIG Networks L2 consensus architecture at [https://github.com/DIG-Network/chia-l2-consensus](https://github.com/DIG-Network/chia-l2-consensus) however the CHIP has been generalized to describe a wider set of use cases.

We achieve this using the following components:

1. An **Election Singleton** that is the canonical registration authority for the epoch and is also the vote finalizer.

2. A **Registration Coin** that voters create by spending the Election Singleton to register to vote for a epoch. This coin holds the voter's CAT collateral and also serves as the on-chain record of the voter's vote — when the voter casts their vote, the registration coin recreates itself with `has_voted=true` and the chosen `vote_data` committed into its curried state, and the voter's BLS signature over the vote message is written into the recreated coin's memos for off-chain aggregation.

   

The lineage proof between the registration coin and its parent Election Singleton spend is what makes the registration legitimate. The vote is legitimate because (a) the registration coin's vote spend emits an `AGG_SIG_UNSAFE` over the standardised vote message — forcing the spend bundle's aggregate signature to include the voter's signature — and (b) the same signature is written into the recreated coin's memos so the off-chain aggregator can extract it without parsing CLVM solutions.

Vote aggregating parties should verify lineage before generating proofs for finalization as a pre-check to ensure their proof bundle will be accepted for finalization.

Vote finalization is achieved by aggregating the votes into a Groth16 circuit off-chain to generate a ZK proof that creates the following commitment: A majority threshold of registered voters contributed to an aggregated BLS signature for a specific message.

CLVM currently has all the required opcodes to verify a Groth16 circuit proof.

## Motivation

**The Problem**

Chia Blockchain is in need of a standard for scalable voting systems. Traditional patterns for voting on Chia involves creating a Singleton on-chain that has a spend path that records a user's vote. The issue with this pattern materializes in how votes are counted. Voting requires a singleton spend, which locks up the singleton for the current block. This forces a one vote per block mechanic which throttles how fast the votes can be counted.  This is commonly referred to as the “Single Parallelism Problem”.  There are some techniques such as Replace-By-Fee (RBF) in conjunction with the Action pattern developed by Yakuhito that enable small scale parallelisation, however, for large scale truly decentralized voting, it could take as many blocks as there are voters to count every vote.

**Why the Election Singleton Matters**

Without canonical registration authority anyone could create a coin with the registration coin puzzle hash and claim to be a registered voter. The Election Singleton solves this in that its a singleton that acts as a gatekeeper for the entire epoch. A registration coin is only valid if lineage proof traces back to a spend of the Election Singleton. Additionally, by spending the Election Singleton to create the registration coin, the inner puzzle can maintain a Sparse Merkle Tree (SPT) of the registration pubkey, maintaining a constant clvm cost mechanism that a pubkey has registered for the epoch.

**Why the Registration Coin Matters**

Even though the Election Singleton maintains a SPT of registered pubkeys, Groth16 circuit proofs are constructed off chain by a vote aggregator. The Aggregator will need to enumerate through the registration coins in the epoch as inputs to the circuit. All registration coins can be queried by hint and it can have its lineage verified to ensure its part of the registered voter set before inputting the vote into the circuit. This helps the vote aggregator ensure that its inputs are valid and they know ahead of time that their proof should be valid.

It additional acts as voter escrow, locking up a 

**Why Groth16**

Groth16 is the most efficient proof system for on-chain verification. It provides a constant-size proof of three elliptic curve point, 192 bytes in total. Verification requires only a handful of pairing checks and point multiplications which are operations CLVM already supports via CHIP-0011

**Technical Feasiblity**

All operators needed for Groth16 verification already exist in CLVM as of CHIP-0011. This CHIP requires no changes to the Chia node or CLVM.

## Backwards Compatibility

This CHIP introduces no changes to CLVM or any existing on-chain primitives. Its is a standards document describing how to use existing operators and how to structure three new puzzle types. There are no backwards compatibility issues.

## Specification

### Definitions

* **Election Singleton**: A Chia singleton that is the canonical registration authority for the epoch. All voter registrations must go through it. One per epoch.  
* **Registration Coin:** A CAT-wrapped coin created by spending the Election Singleton. Holds the voter's CAT collateral. Only valid if its lineage proof traces back to an Election Singleton coinspend. It has 2 spend paths: vote (recreates the coin with `has_voted=true` and the chosen `vote_data` committed into curried state) and release_collateral (sends the CAT collateral to a destination, only valid after the epoch has been finalized in the Election Singleton). The voter's BLS signature over the vote message is written into the recreated coin's memos so off-chain aggregators can extract it efficiently. Collateral must be in the form of a Governance CAT. A Governance Token specification is outside the scope of this CHIP.  
* **Lineage Proof**: The chain of parent coin IDs proving that a registration coin was created through the Election Singleton.  
* **Epoch**: This is the vote session, it is the period of time between when the Election Singleton was created on chain and when the vote has been finalized.  
* **Sparse Merkle Tree**: A fixed-depth (32) Merkle tree where each voter has a deterministic slot derived from `sha256(pubkey)`, supporting registration proofs.  
* **Groth16 proof**: Three BLS12-381 curve points (A: G1 48 bytes, B: G2 96 bytes, C: G1 48 bytes). 192 bytes total.  
* **Verification Key**: BLS12-381 curve points from the trusted setup (672 bytes total: alpha\_g1 \+ beta\_g2 \+ gamma\_g2 \+ delta\_g2 \+ 7 IC points) curried into the Election Singleton at deployment.

### Summary

Creating a decentralized voting scheme on Chia that scales to an unbounded number of voters requires the following properties:

1. Our puzzle must maintain a known voter set, we can not prove voter threshold if we are not tracking total number of possible voters.  
2. We must be able to aggregate the votes off chain, its infeasible to aggregate votes of unbounded participants in CLVM with block size limits and CLVM costs being hard walls.  
3. Anyone should be able to submit a vote proof, there should not be a designated party who is in charge of submitting the vote on chain.  
4. CLVM should be able to verify if the vote proof is valid or not and it should not be forgable.  
5. The proof must be constant size so that CLVM costs are uncorrelated with voter count.

Aggregated BLS Signatures alone are insufficient, they can aggregate signers, but they don't maintain a concept of who signed or how many signed. Groth16 is a constant size proof that can be verified using existing CLVM opcodes and it allows us to encode the required information to verify the proof was unforged and the vote is finalized. 

## **Groth16 Voter Consensus Explained**

Using a Groth16 circuit we can prove that the minimum required signers have participated by building an agreement curve into the circuit. An agreement curve works as a threshold indicator by looking at the number of curve shapes intercept with the proof anchor. The circuit is constructed in such a way that when the number of signers is below the signer threshold, the curve becomes ambiguous, it contains multiple curve solutions that intercepts the proof anchor.

![Figure 1](./assets/figure_1.png)


Once the threshold has been reached, only a single curve solution incepts the proof anchor. The threshold can be configured into the circuit, it could be structured as a majority threshold (51%+) or a quorum (60%+). Once the threshold of signers is met, any set of signers above the threshold will produce a valid proof.

![Figure 2](./assets/figure_2.png)  

### Voter Set Construction

When aggregating votes the submitter:

1. Queries all the coins with the registration coin puzzle mode hash on Chia and verified the lineage back to the Election Singleton.  
2. Constructs a sparse merkle tree from verified registration coins only.  
3. Reads the current Election Singleton state  
4. Collects k voter signatures over the vote message where `2k > registration_count`  
5. Computes `agg_sig` (G2 aggregate) and `agg_signers` (G1 aggregate).  
6. Generates k Merkle inclusion proofs.  
7. Runs the Groth16 prover.  
8. Builds and broadcasts the vote finalization spend bundle.  
   

### Sparse Merkle Tree

The sparse Merkle tree has fixed depth 32, supporting 2^32 registration slots. Each voter registration occupies a slot derived from their public key:

`slot = first_8_bytes_as_u64_big_endian(sha256(pubkey)) mod 2^32`

Leaf Values:

* Active Leaf: `sha256(pubkey)` (48-byte compressed G1 input)  
* Empty leag: `sha256([0x00; 48])` \= `EMPTY_LEAF_HASH`

The tree root is computed as `sha256(left || right)` at each level, with left child always first. Empty subtrees use precomputed hashes for efficiency.

### Circuit Public Inputs

The Groth16 circuit accepts exactly 6 inputs in fixed order:

1. `registration_merkle_root` \- current active set root  
2. `registration_count` \- current count  
3. `agg_signers` \- G1 aggregate of k signing pubkeys  
4. `vote_message` \- sha256 of the new state fields \+ network Id

### Circuit Statement

\> I know k pubkeys, each with a valid Merkle inclusion proof against  
\> `registration_merkle_root`, whose G1 sum equals `agg_signers`, and where  
\> `2k > registration_count`

The circuit enforces three constraints:

1. **Merkle membership**: Each signer has a valid inclusion proof  
2. **Aggregate key binding**: G1 sum of k pubkeys \== `agg_signers`\`   
   This prevents a phantom majority attack where an attacker forces a proof claiming more signers then actually exist.  
3. **Majority threshold**: `2k > registration_count`  
   

Circuit parameters fixed at trusted setup:

1. `MAX_SIGNERS` \= 20,000  
2. `TREE_DEPTH` \= 32

### Groth16 On-Chain Verification

A Groth16 proof `(A, B, C)` is verified by the equation

`e(A, B) * e(-vk_alpha, vk_beta) * e(-vk_input, vk_gamma) * e(-C, vk_delta) = 1`

Where `vk_input` is commuted using `g1_multiply` and `point_add` from the public inputs, IC points and scalar values. Each scaler is `sha256(public_input)` interpreted as a big-endian integer.

## Election Singleton

The Election Singleton is a singleton that acts as the canonical gatekeeper for voter registration and it acts as the vote finalizer. There is typically exactly one Election Singleton per vote.

The Election Singleton also defines a registration fee, this is a fee, in XCH that is required to register to vote. It is reserved as a reward for the finalizer. Anyone can compute a valid proof and submit to be the finalizer. This creates an economic mechanism to finalize the Election Singleton as fast as possible as soon as the threshold is met. The registration fee should be nominal enough that its minimal per registration, but in aggregate, adds up to something worth spending the block inclusion fees on Chia.

The Election Singleton also defines `ELECTION_LENGTH_BLOCKS`, an L1 block count curried into the singleton at deployment. The finalize spend path emits `ASSERT_HEIGHT_RELATIVE(ELECTION_LENGTH_BLOCKS)`, which means the finalize spend can only succeed once at least `ELECTION_LENGTH_BLOCKS` L1 blocks have passed since the singleton coin currently being spent was created. Because every register spend recreates the singleton, this requires `ELECTION_LENGTH_BLOCKS` of quiet (no new registrations) before a finalize is permitted. Without this delay there is a bootstrap attack: at the very beginning of the election there are zero registered voters, so the first registrant could immediately satisfy the majority threshold (`2*1 > 1`) and finalize the vote unilaterally. Spamming registrations to indefinitely delay finalization is economically self-limiting because every registration costs `REGISTRATION_FEE`, and that fee is paid out as the eventual finalizer's reward.

The inner puzzle has six curried parameters and two solution parameters:

\`\`\`rue

\`\`\`

### Registration Coin

The registration coin holds the voter’s collateral and commits to their public key. It can only be spent when the Election Singleton is in its finalization state, releasing the collateral. Collateral should be in the form of a Governance CAT token. The weight of the vote is a function on the amount of collateral locked up.

The puzzle has four curried parameters and three solution parameters. No conditions pass-through is permitted to prevent condition injection.

\`\`\`rue  
\`\`\`

### Vote Path on the Registration Coin

The registration coin's vote spend path is what casts the voter's vote. Only one vote per registration coin is allowed (enforced by the `has_voted` flag in curried state — once flipped to `true`, the recreated coin's puzzle hash changes and the same vote spend can never be replayed). The vote is weighed by the amount of CAT collateral locked up for this Epoch. Binding the vote weight to the governance token lockup creates a disincentive to split and register tokens across multiple pubkeys.

The vote spend recreates the registration coin with the new state (`has_voted=true`, `vote_data` set to the voter's choice) and writes `(vote_data, vote_signature)` into the recreated coin's memos. Off-chain vote aggregators query registration coins by per-voter hint = `sha256("CHIP/onchain/voter_hint/v1/" || election_launcher_id || cat_tail_hash || voter_pubkey)` (see `puzzles::voter_hint`), fetch each coin's parent spend, extract `vote_data` and `vote_signature` from the memos, verify the signature against the standardised vote message, and aggregate the verified BLS signatures for the Election Singleton's finalize input.

## Security

**Lineage proof enforcement**: A registration coin is only valid if its parent coin ID traces back to an Election Singleton coinspend. This is enforced by the circuit.

**Two-check consensus**: The ZK proof alone does prove that the signature was made. Conversely, the aggregated signature does not prove that the quorum was legitimate. Together they prove the complete guarantee.

**Aggregate key binding**: The circuit enforces that `agg_signers` equals the G1 sum of the k signing pubkeys. This prevents phantom majority attacks where an attacker with the proving key forges a proof claiming an arbitrary number of signers.

**Collateral Security**: A voter can not recover their collateral until the epoch is finalized. This prevents an attacker from voting, withdrawing their collateral and voting again under a different pubkey.

**Bootstrap Attack Prevention**: The finalize spend path on the Election Singleton enforces `ASSERT_HEIGHT_RELATIVE(ELECTION_LENGTH_BLOCKS)`. Without this delay, the very first registrant could vote and immediately finalize alone (because `2k > registration_count` is trivially satisfied when `k = registration_count = 1`). With the delay, finalization is only permitted after a quiet window of `ELECTION_LENGTH_BLOCKS` since the most recent registration. An attacker attempting to delay finalization by spamming registrations must pay `REGISTRATION_FEE` per spam registration, all of which accrues to the eventual finalizer's reward — making the attack self-defeating.

**Trusted Setup**: Groth16 requires a one-time trusted setup per circuit configuration. Applications MUST conduct a multi-party computation (MPC) ceremony. A single-party setup MUST NOT be used in production. If the setup is compromised, an attacker can generate fake proofs. At least one honest participant in the MPC ceremony is sufficient for soundness.
